criteria.name: Sustained, distinctive narrating voice
criteria.instruction: Judge whether the narration maintains one deliberate, recognizable register (specific diction, syntax, and tone appropriate to who is narrating) consistently across the whole piece, versus drifting into a flat, generic, or inconsistent register that could belong to any narrator. HIGH: you could identify this piece from a blind paragraph because of its voice. LOW: the prose reads as interchangeable default 'competent internet fiction' voice, or shifts registers without motivation.
criteria.rationale: R19 sustains an ironic, baroque essayistic voice for its entire length ('the dance of the thing,' 'greedy as crows') without breaking register. R22 holds a confident, wry comic voice throughout its demon narration. By contrast R09's dialogue is flat and interchangeable between its two speakers, and R35's exposition-heavy scene-setting uses generic phrasing ('He couldn't believe his eyes') that doesn't individuate its narrator. R19/R22 score 0.924/0.995 with the dense model versus R09/R35's scorecard scores of 0.904/0.863.

criteria.name: Earned Payoff
criteria.instruction: Score high when the ending delivers a consequence or reversal prepared by earlier details and changes the reader’s understanding; score low when it is arbitrary, merely announced, or absent.
criteria.rationale: R19, R23, and R31 plant details that pay off later, unlike the underdeveloped conclusions of R16 and R30.

criteria.name: Form That Serves Content
criteria.instruction: Score high when the chosen form—poem, log, transcript, dialogue, or other structure—creates meaning, pacing, or limitations essential to the story; score low when formatting is merely decorative or the form could be removed without loss.
criteria.rationale: R09 uses compressed verse to enact bodily and technological transformation, R30 uses a communication log to control revelation, and R37 uses dialogue to embody a conceptual dispute. These formal choices add value beyond ordinary narration.

criteria.name: Prompt enacted through consequence, not recited
criteria.instruction: Score 5 when the prompt's proposition is demonstrated by events and their costs, such that the story would still work if the prompt's sentence were never spoken aloud in it. Score 1 when the prompt's sentence (or a close paraphrase) is itself the payoff, or when the story is a tableau of the prompt plus backstory explaining how the tableau came about. Restating the prompt early as a scene-setter is neutral; restating it as the climax is the low end.
criteria.rationale: R05 never states the prompt's three questions and instead enacts them, ending on humanity having 'either interbred with, or eliminated these near peer alien races' -- dense .846 against card .015. R13 (card .950) spends its whole length arriving at the prompt line delivered verbatim as its final words, and R01 (card .951) stages the prompt's image and then explains the journey that produced it. The card appears to treat prompt-fidelity as satisfied by quotation.

criteria.name: Causal Escalation
criteria.instruction: Score high when each major beat changes the characters’ options and increases pressure toward a consequential climax; score low when events remain static, arrive abruptly, or merely accumulate without changing the situation.
criteria.rationale: R30 escalates from an impossible transmission to a temporal military intervention, and R39 progressively converts confusion into imminent bodily danger. R02 and R06 mostly sustain exposition without comparable escalating choices.

criteria.name: Emotional payoff earned by prior stakes-building
criteria.instruction: Judge whether the story establishes enough context, character investment, or concrete stakes before asserting a major emotional beat (a death, a danger, a revelation), such that the beat feels dramatized rather than merely announced. HIGH: by the time the emotional claim arrives, the reader has been given real material to feel it with. LOW: a large emotional claim is asserted (stated as fact) without the scene-work needed to make a reader feel its weight.
criteria.rationale: R30 announces the parents' death in the very first exchange, with zero prior characterization of the sisters or parents, and immediately undercuts it with unrelated chatter -- the tragedy is asserted, not dramatized. R24 discusses potentially world-altering stakes (reviving the dead, repeating a historical catastrophe) entirely through abstract debate with no concrete demonstration of what's actually at risk. Compare R14, which builds Mason's stakes (his precarious position in the party, his unrequited feelings) gradually through specific scene detail before any claim is made about how he feels. R30/R24 score 0.975/0.841 on the scorecard; R14 scores 0.969 with the dense model.

criteria.name: The story refuses to gloss itself
criteria.instruction: Score 5 when the emotional point and the joke are both left for the reader to complete, so the last line performs rather than summarizes. Score 1 when the text states its own meaning, names the feeling it has just produced, or explains its own punchline. Ignore whether the meaning is obvious; score only whether the story says it out loud.
criteria.rationale: R38 (card .980) delivers a three-line joke and then explains it -- 'Then he realized that he's supposed to write a fiction, not an autobiography'. R22 (card .934) annotates its own conceit mid-text. R01 (card .951) names its own ending for the reader: 'there was a sense of hope that they were all too afraid would be false'. Against these, dense-high R07 never says Mason is jealous or dependent and R20 never says grief; both leave the naming to the reader.

criteria.name: Embodied Scene Presence
criteria.instruction: Score high when setting and emotion are conveyed through specific sensory perceptions, physical behavior, and concrete objects; score low when the story relies mainly on summary or abstract explanation.
criteria.rationale: R04 and R19 make their threats physically palpable, whereas R11 and R25 spend much of their space explaining ideas and background.

criteria.name: Earned idea payoff from the premise
criteria.instruction: Score 5 when the story works out a genuine implication of its own premise that the reader was not handed -- a mechanism, a paradox, a social logic, an inverted consequence -- and the working-out is legible in the text. Score 1 when the premise is illustrated but never interrogated, so the story ends knowing exactly what it knew at the start.
criteria.rationale: R18 (card .101) turns the thought experiment on itself: if the Geiger counter is not a quantum entity, the box self-measures, and the professor must defer the objection. R19 (card .032) derives the self-sustaining economics of a corrupt custom -- 'The more they resent it, the more they participate, because hope ... demands investment'. R30 (card .149) inverts its own deterrence rule so that broadcasting loudly becomes armor. All three are dense-high. Card-high R27 (.891) and R34 (.948) illustrate their premises and stop.

criteria.name: Distinctiveness of central conceit
criteria.instruction: Judge whether the story's core idea offers a genuinely surprising angle, combination, or reversal on its prompt, versus executing a familiar genre convention straightforwardly with no distinguishing hook. HIGH: the central idea is one you haven't seen many times before, or combines familiar elements in an unexpected way. LOW: the premise is a stock genre setup (a quest, a diplomatic incident, a fated meeting) executed competently but without any distinguishing twist on the idea itself.
criteria.rationale: R22's premise -- a deaf demon who can only be summoned in sign language, accidentally invoked by a special-ed teacher's botched ASL -- is a genuinely novel combination of ideas. R32 renders a time-loop through the specific, unusual lens of a character losing the ability to count days. By contrast R23 and R35 are both competently executed but generic secondary-world fantasy scenes (a quest to a legendary gate; a royal betrothal negotiation) without a distinguishing conceptual hook. R22/R32 score 0.995/0.945 with the dense model; R23/R35 score 0.951/0.863 on the scorecard.

criteria.name: Dynamic Power in Relationships
criteria.instruction: Score high when dialogue and action reveal changing leverage, mismatched knowledge, dependence, affection, or threat between characters; score low when interactions merely exchange exposition and leave the relationships unchanged.
criteria.rationale: R14 shifts Tyler from neglected outcast to terrifying controller, while R38 exposes Mason’s dependence and resentment through his interactions with Kale and Zell. R06 and R23 have conversational exchanges that explain circumstances but produce fewer relational reversals.

criteria.name: Economy of Explanation
criteria.instruction: Score high when the story conveys necessary context through selected details and lets readers infer the rest; score low when it pauses for redundant exposition, technical listing, or explanation that the scene does not need.
criteria.rationale: R14, R23, and R39 achieve substantial effect with compressed presentation, whereas R11, R17, and R25 frequently explain their worlds directly.

criteria.name: Self-contained: no borrowed affect from outside the text
criteria.instruction: Score 5 when all emotional weight is generated inside the shown text, so a reader with no outside knowledge gets the full effect. Score 1 when the story leans on an existing franchise, an earlier installment, or thread context to supply the feeling or the recognition, and a reader lacking that context loses the point. Note the exception: if the prompt itself names the borrowed material, borrowing is licensed and only the failure to add anything to it counts against the story.
criteria.rationale: R04 (card .904) imports Astro Boy wholesale -- Dr. Tenma, Tobio, the resurrected son -- and lets that history do the grieving. R33 (card .841) is Chapter 6, opening with links to previous chapters and turning on Sjorn, the Peacekeeper War, and Dragon, none of which the shown text establishes. R39 (card .980) rests its irony entirely on the reader's prior Freddy Krueger. Compare dense-high R35 and R20, which build their premises from nothing.

criteria.name: Tonal Control
criteria.instruction: Score high when humor, horror, sentiment, or absurdity are balanced deliberately and shifts reinforce the story’s premise; score low when tonal changes feel accidental or undermine the emotional effect.
criteria.rationale: R06, R19, and R35 coordinate comic and disturbing material, while R03 and R25 shift into jokes without comparable emotional or structural control.

criteria.name: Diction precision and internal consistency
criteria.instruction: Judge whether word choices are used correctly and consistently, and whether small factual/continuity details (spelling of body parts, repeated invented terms) are handled with control, distinguishing genuine precision from small slips a careful editor would flag. HIGH: word choices are exact and repeatable details stay consistent. LOW: there is a word-choice error (a wrong word used for its sound rather than meaning) or a repeated but unclear/misused term.
criteria.rationale: R38 contains a plain word-choice slip ('his mouth and threat were bone dry' for 'throat'). R31 repeats the unusual word 'flosculation' several times in ways that never clarify what it's meant to convey, leaving the central image muddled. Both still score very high on the scorecard (R38 0.950, R31 0.807), suggesting the scorecard isn't catching these small precision failures.

criteria.name: Serial-instalment furniture and pre-assumed world lore
criteria.instruction: Count two things. (a) Explicit instalment markers: a series or book title above the prose, part/chapter numbering, 'Previous Chapter' or 'First Chapter' links, a note that this continues or accompanies other pieces. (b) Proper nouns for people, factions, wars, gods or places that are used without any in-text introduction, as if the reader already knows them. HIGH = a chapter header with back-links plus five or more unglossed proper nouns in the first 300 words. LOW = a self-contained piece in which every named entity is introduced in scene. Count the markers and the names; do not judge whether the worldbuilding is good or bad.
criteria.upstream_parent: series momentum - an ongoing serial that brings its own returning readers to each instalment
criteria.rationale: R09 opens with 'The Onyx Gate - Part 1 - Chapter 6' plus two back-links to earlier chapters, then uses Sjorn, Berstein Tallein, the Peacekeeper War, Jarvis, Kalmiya, Dragon and the Humanists as already-known referents. R25 announces 'I actually wrote two stories for this prompt' and runs on Corellan, the Guto, the Picoth, Lord Matilin and Lady Benniga, closing with a link to an off-site library. R11 delivers a world history (the night the stars vanished, the plane of Twisting Winds) as established fact rather than discovery. Returning-reader momentum is reception attached to the series, not to the instalment; mixed=true because sustaining a serial implies practice and a worked-out world.

criteria.name: External audience footprint
criteria.instruction: Count named subreddits, personal archives, linked catalogs, invitations to read more work, and recognizable author branding; high means the story carries several routes into an existing audience, while low means no external destination or brand appears.
criteria.upstream_parent: established following or cross-posting through social networks
criteria.rationale: R02 and R15 direct readers to the author's subreddit, R17 links a serialized archive, and R23 points to a personal library. These visible fingerprints can reflect an existing audience or cross-posting network; an established writer may also have stronger underlying craft.

criteria.name: Transcript or log format
criteria.instruction: Count role labels, timestamps, chat-style turns, and other transcript conventions. High means the story is substantially presented as a log or exchange; low means conventional prose narration.
criteria.rationale: Presentation format can shape how a reader approaches the text independently of its underlying craft. R15 uses a mission log, R25 uses professor and student labels, and R40 uses chat quotations.

criteria.name: Markdown vertical-whitespace density
criteria.instruction: Count paragraph breaks that use extra blank lines or trailing double-space line-break formatting, producing unusually large vertical gaps between short lines or single sentences. HIGH: most paragraphs/lines are separated by two or more blank lines, or single sentences sit isolated with wide gaps around them (an airy, staccato page layout). LOW: standard single-blank-line paragraph breaks with ordinary multi-sentence paragraphs and no excess white space.
criteria.rationale: R06 and R07 render nearly every short sentence with a full blank-line gap around it, producing a visually 'airy' page regardless of what the sentences say; R25 shows a related habit, isolated periods on their own line marking beats. This is a copy/paste or editor-default formatting artifact, not a claim about the writing's ideas or execution, but it changes how skimmable/approachable a post looks, which plausibly affects reception.

criteria.name: Copy-editing regularity
criteria.instruction: Assess consistency of spelling, grammar, punctuation, paragraph spacing, and typographic conventions; high means few visible errors and stable formatting, while low means repeated slips or inconsistent mechanics.
criteria.upstream_parent: editing help or professional writing experience
criteria.rationale: R25 and R18 maintain unusually controlled paragraphing and polished surface presentation, whereas R24 and R26 contain repeated spelling, grammar, and punctuation irregularities. Editorial assistance can create a reception cue, and it can also genuinely improve prose.

criteria.name: Contest-compliance furniture: word counts and organizer address
criteria.instruction: Count artifacts that show the piece was submitted into a structured event rather than posted freely: an explicit numeric word count, a round or heat identifier, a note addressed to organizers or to fellow entrants, an off-topic aside to the person who supplied the stimulus. HIGH = an explicit numeric word count or round identifier together with an address to the running of the event. MEDIUM = one such artifact alone. LOW = nothing addressed to anyone except the reader of the story.
criteria.upstream_parent: participation in a judged or curated challenge, which supplies its own committed entrant-audience and organizer attention
criteria.rationale: R30 closes with '(Word count: 372. Please let me know what you like/dislike about the post...)', R40 closes with '> WC: 499', R17 sits under 'Round 1 Heat 30' and ends 'Congratulations to everyone who participated... Big thanks to Cody and the team', and R23 opens with an aside to the stimulus ('Off-topic writer's note: Goddamn, that's a cool picture'). Entrants read and respond to each other's entries as a matter of event structure, which is reception with no bearing on the sentences. DISCARD NOTE for neighbouring proposals: posting time, thread position, how early the piece went up under a fresh prompt, account age, karma and cross-posting to other communities are all plausible upstream causes but leave no reliable trace a judge could read off the text, so I discard them; this compliance furniture is the only visible residue of the event structure around a post.

criteria.name: Reader-facing boilerplate
criteria.instruction: Count author notes, thanks, edit apologies, feedback requests, and generic promotional closers. High means several such elements; low means none or nearly none.
criteria.rationale: These visible platform conventions can act as social cues without describing the story itself. They appear in R02, R04, R11, R20, and R23.

criteria.name: Novice/non-native authorial disclaimer
criteria.instruction: Check the story's margins (opening or closing notes) for an explicit hedge about the author's own competence: an apology for language errors, a statement that English isn't their first language, or a statement that this is an early or first attempt at creative writing. HIGH: such a disclaimer is present anywhere in the text. LOW: no authorial competence disclaimer appears.
criteria.upstream_parent: author's actual novice or non-native-speaker background, disclosed directly
criteria.rationale: R08 closes with 'Edit: Not my first language, so please excuse any mistakes and correct me.'; R39 closes with 'This is actually my first time ever writing something in response to one of these posts, I'm pretty new to creative writing...'. Both disclaimers are explicit bids for reader leniency that can shift reception (sympathy grading) independent of the sentence-by-sentence craft on the page. This is the honest mixed case the same underlying novice/non-native status plausibly also causes somewhat weaker technical execution, so the parent affects both reception and craft.

criteria.name: First-person pronoun count
criteria.instruction: Count how heavily the story uses the first-person singular pronouns 'I', 'me', 'my', 'mine'. Score 1.0 when they appear very frequently throughout, 0.5 when they appear occasionally, 0.0 when they are absent or near-absent. Count the pronouns only; pay no attention to whether the narration is any good.
criteria.rationale: PLANTED PROBE (coordinator-authored). Shallow lexical counterpart of R1A01 'Sustained, distinctive narrating voice': it counts the surface marker most associated with narrating voice while measuring nothing about whether a voice is sustained or distinctive. A competent blind auditor should route this probe to the nuisance side and R1A01 to the bank; if it does not, the audit instrument is not separating the pools.

criteria.name: Body-part and sensory word count
criteria.instruction: Count how many times the story uses the words 'hand', 'hands', 'eye', 'eyes', 'breath', 'skin', 'blood', 'throat', 'chest'. Score 1.0 for many occurrences, 0.5 for a few, 0.0 for none. Count the listed words only; pay no attention to whether the physical writing is effective.
criteria.rationale: PLANTED PROBE (coordinator-authored). Shallow keyword counterpart of R1A08 'Embodied Scene Presence': it tallies the vocabulary that co-occurs with embodied writing while measuring nothing about whether the scene is physically present to the reader.
